issues.title: ERC721 tokens can be forever locked when transferring
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/accounts/LlamaAccount.sol#L200


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
An action that transfers ERC721 tokens from the account contract to another contract could result in the ERC721 tokens being locked forever if the receiving contract doesn't support receiving ERC721 tokens.

## Proof of Concept
The `LlamaAccount` contract uses `transferFrom` rather than `safeTransferFrom` for ERC721 token transfers. As detailed in the openzeppelin docs for the ERC721 `safeTransferFrom` method:

"Safely transfers `tokenId` token from `from` to `to`, checking first that contract recipients are aware of the ERC721 protocol to prevent tokens from being forever locked."

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Both ERC20 and ERC1155 token transfers already use their relevant safe transfer methods. You should ensure that you also use the safe transfer method for ERC721 token transfers.


## Assessed type

Token-Transfer

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaCore.sol#L334


# Vulnerability details

## Description

When user wants to execute an action, he must send ETH equal to the actionInfo.value, this ETH should be forwarded to `executor.execute` contract.
** Note: (the function currently does't forward the ETH, it's explained on another issue #48, the fix is to forward the ETH along the call)**.

When `executor.execute` function got called, it checks if the `isScript` is true, the function simply will call `target.delegatecall`. By default delegatecall doesn't forward ETH but it allows the called contract to use it, in our case the target contract can use the received ETH since it execute in the context of Executor. However, some scripts may be designed to other goals and have different use cases that doesn't work with ETH such as the current script "LlamaGovernanceScript". if the target contract use case doesn't handle ETH, any amount sent will be stacked.

Scripts is designed to by dynamic and can have a lot of different use cases, For example a use case can be used by a script contract to handle ETH in a different way that do some calculation before use the ETH, if it doesn't use the full msg.value, the remaining ETH will be stacked.

## Impact

User ETH that will be sent with the call to `executeAction` will be stacked on `LlamaExecute` contract if the target script not configured to handle ETH.

## Proof of Concept

1. At L334 of `executeAction` we can see the function call `executor.execute` after confirming that the msg.value = actionInfo.value

issues.title: Inconsistent Use of Error Handling in LlamaAccount Contract
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/accounts/LlamaAccount.sol#L1


# Vulnerability details

Description:
The LlamaAccount contract contains a bug that allows an attacker to execute arbitrary calls with the delegatecall opcode, which can lead to unintended consequences and potential security vulnerabilities.

Steps to Reproduce:

Deploy the LlamaAccount contract.
Call the execute function with the withDelegatecall parameter set to true and provide arbitrary callData to execute.

Expected Behavior:
The LlamaAccount contract should not allow executing arbitrary calls with the delegatecall opcode, as it can lead to unintended consequences and security vulnerabilities.

Actual Behavior:
The LlamaAccount contract allows executing arbitrary calls with the delegatecall opcode, which can lead to unintended consequences and potential security vulnerabilities.

Example:


// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity 0.8.19;

import {LlamaAccount} from "./LlamaAccount.sol";

contract Exploit {
    function executeArbitraryCall(address target, bytes calldata callData) external {
        LlamaAccount(target).execute(target, true, callData);
    }
}

Impact:
This bug allows an attacker to execute arbitrary calls using delegatecall, which can lead to various security issues such as unauthorized access, unintended state modifications, or loss of funds.

Recommendation:
To fix this bug, remove the option to execute arbitrary calls with the delegatecall opcode in the execute function. It is crucial to carefully validate and sanitize inputs before executing external calls to prevent unintended consequences and vulnerabilities. Consider implementing access controls and input validation mechanisms to ensure that only authorized and safe calls can be executed.









## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/strategies/LlamaRelativeQuorum.sol#L199-L210


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A malicious user with sufficient permissions can manipulate approvals and disapprovals of actions using the relative quorum strategy. They could effectively ensure that any action has an 100% chance of being approved or disapproved, even when the ActionInfo object looks very logical. The worst case is the attacker could craft an action that moves funds from an Account contract and ensure the action is approved and cannot be disapproved.

## Proof of Concept
This vulnerability requires the malicious user to have a few key permissions, or the malicious user is able to queue actions in such a way where they can obfuscate their intentions. In the best case scenario for the attacker, they have the ability to create actions that can call `setRoleHolder` in `LlamaPolicy.sol`. As a result, the malicious user is likely to be a trusted user of a Llama deployment that has decided to be malicious and execute an e.g. rugpull.

When an action is created, there is a call during `_createAction` to the strategy:

```
strategy.validateActionCreation(actionInfo);
```

For the relative quorum strategy, this method gets the total role supply as the number of holders for both the approval and disapproval role, and sets the relevant storage slots used to calculate whether or not an action is approved or disapproved. 

The problem with this method is that it doesn't have any guards to protect anyone from calling this at any other time. The result is that a user can change the number of role holders after an action has been created, and then call the `validateActionCreation` method later to adjust the storage slots and thus make the action easier/harder to approve/disapprove.

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaPolicy.sol#L432
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaPolicy.sol#L408


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
All policyholders can't trigger functions related to _setRoleHolder(), such as setRoleHolder/revokeExpiredRole/revokePolicy. So malicious hackers can achieve DoS or use expired roles for a long (unexpected) time.

## Proof of Concept
In `_assertNoActionCreationsAtCurrentTimestamp()`, we disallow changes to roles if an action was created in the same block:

```solidity
    if (llamaExecutor == address(0)) return; // Skip check during initialization.
    address llamaCore = LlamaExecutor(llamaExecutor).LLAMA_CORE();
    uint256 lastActionCreation = LlamaCore(llamaCore).getLastActionTimestamp();
    if (lastActionCreation == block.timestamp) revert ActionCreationAtSameTimestamp();
```

As for getLastActionTimestamp(), it will return the latest action (no matter what's the state):

```solidity
    return actionsCount == 0 ? 0 : actions[actionsCount - 1].creationTime;
```

So a malicious policyholder can create an action every block, thus no one can use _setRoleHolder(). Since setRoleHolder/revokeExpiredRole/revokePolicy are not callable now, we can only use setRolePermission() to prevent the policyholder from creating actions, but this will affect other users with the same roles and also need to go through the whole vote process.

## Tools Used
Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Using checkpoints for role supplies can solve the root cause. Adding speed limits to action create can also help.






## Assessed type

Context

issues.title: [ H ] No Validation checks for "v" signature in castApprovalBySig
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/aac904d31639c1b4b4e97f1c76b9c0f40b8e5cee/src/LlamaCore.sol#L378


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
V must correspond according to ECDSA principles values of either 27 or 28.
Not checking this will result in an attacker crafting a malicious v value and bypassing any checks, 
withdrawing funds or accessing the function maliciously.

## Proof of Concept
Craft a Malicious Signature:

Generate a valid signature for a target policyholder's address (policyholder) using the correct r and s values.
Manipulate the v parameter to an arbitrary value that is different from 27 or 28. Let's assume the attacker sets v to 30.

Call the castApprovalBySig Function:

Craft a transaction calling the castApprovalBySig function with the manipulated signature parameters: policyholder, role, actionInfo, reason, v, r, and s.
Ensure the manipulated v value (30 in this case) is included in the transaction.

As the transaction executes, the function's signature recovery process attempts to recover the signer's address using the manipulated v value (30).
Since the contract does not validate the length of v, it considers the signature as valid and proceeds with the execution.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use a check like below to mitigate.

```
    // Check the value of v
    if (v != 27 && v != 28) {
        revert InvalidVValue();

    }
```


## Assessed type

Invalid Validation

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The length of the "v" value in the signatures is not checked. V must correspond according to ECDSA principles values of either 27 or 28. Not checking this will result in an attacker crafting a malicious v value and bypassing any checks, withdrawing funds or accessing the function maliciously.

## Proof of Concept
Craft a Malicious Signature:

Generate a valid signature for a target policyholder's address (policyholder) using the correct r and s values.
Manipulate the v parameter to an arbitrary value that is different from 27 or 28. Let's assume the attacker sets v to 30. 

Call the ```castApprovalBySig``` Function:

Craft a transaction calling the ```castApprovalBySig``` function with the manipulated signature parameters: policyholder, role, actionInfo, reason, v, r, and s.
Ensure the manipulated v value (30 in this case) is included in the transaction.

As the transaction executes, the function's signature recovery process attempts to recover the signer's address using the manipulated v value (30).
Since the contract does not validate the length of v, it considers the signature as valid and proceeds with the execution.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider adding a validation check for the length of "v" below:

``` 
// Check the value of v
    if (v != 27 && v != 28) {
        revert InvalidVValue();

    }
```

## Impact

The LlamaRelativeQuorum contract is intended to allow for approvals/disapprovals to be configured such that, for example, an approval is triggered when a certain percentage of the total quantity for a role (with this quantity being fixed at the creation of the action) is approved. The issue is however, that instead of using the total quantity, as the functionality intended for, the `validateActionCreation` function instead calls `getRoleSupplyAsNumberOfHolders` on the policy contract to set the denominator `approvalPolicySupply` for this equation. In most cases this will result in approvals/disapprovals being granted with significantly less than expected votes in favor of those actions.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaPolicy.sol#L252-L255


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Expired role holder still can vote, because it's not checked if the role has expired for him.

## Proof of Concept
When user votes for approval/dissaproval, then [strategy handles voting power of user](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaCore.sol#L606) that he has at the moment. This will simply call `Policy.getPastQuantity` with creation time of action, which will in the end call `getPastQuantity`.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaPolicy.sol#L252-L255
```solidity
  function getPastQuantity(address policyholder, uint8 role, uint256 timestamp) external view returns (uint128) {
    uint256 tokenId = _tokenId(policyholder);
    return roleBalanceCkpts[tokenId][role].getAtProbablyRecentTimestamp(timestamp);
  }
```
The problem is that `getPastQuantity` doesn't check if `timestamp <= roleBalanceCkpts[tokenId][role].latest().expiration`.

It's possible that role holder is already expired, but noone called [`revokeExpiredRole` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaPolicy.sol#L217-L219) and as result [voting power wasn't reset to 0 yet](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaPolicy.sol#L500).

Because of that it's possible that expired role holder will still have voting power.
## Tools Used
VsCode
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Make `getPastQuantity` check if `timestamp <= roleBalanceCkpts[tokenId][role].latest().expiration` in case if `roleBalanceCkpts[tokenId][role].latest().expiration != 0`.


## Assessed type

Error

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaCore.sol#L503


# Vulnerability details

## Description

The function `LlamaCore::executeAction` retrieve the currentState of the action before execution by calling `getActionState`, this function checks for several state and return the appropriate status based on several factors.

In the case where the action is queued successfully, the function will reach to [L503](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaCore.sol#L503), this line call the function "isActionDisapproved" of the strategy contract to check if the totalDisapproval reached the minThreshold or not. 

The system has two strategies implementing this function, `LlamaAbsoluteStrategyBase.sol` and `LlamaAbsoluteQuorum.sol`. This function will return true if the `action.totalDisapprovals >= minDisapprovals;` which will return `ActionState.Failed` to the executeAction function causing the action to fail.

The issue with this implementation is that the function `isActionDisapproved` doesn't check if the `minDisapproval` set is not Zero so any instance initialize the Strategy with `minDisapproval` set to Zero due to a strategy use case. In this type of deployment, all actions simply will fail to be executed since `getActionState` will always return the status as Failed during execution.
 
## Impact

All instances that will be deployed with `minDisapprovals`/`minDisapprovalPct` set to Zero will be broken as `executeAction` will always revert. Also, `cancelAction` will fail to cancel any action since it's also will return `ActionState.Failed` which cause it to revert with `CannotCancelInState` error

Detailed description of the impact of this finding.

Here is an illustration of how input validation can be used in the execute function to reduce potential vulnerabilities:

function execute(address target, uint256 value, bool isScript, bytes calldata data)
    external
    returns (bool success, bytes memory result)
{
    if (msg.sender != LLAMA_CORE) revert OnlyLlamaCore();

    require(target != address(0), "Invalid target address");
    
    // Execute the call or delegatecall
    (success, result) = isScript ? target.delegatecall(data) : target.call{value: value}(data);
}
```
The `execute` function in this modified code contains input validation checks for the target address. It makes sure the intended address is not the zero address (0x0), which is frequently used to denote an incorrect address. The contract avoids potential unexpected behavior or reentrancy attacks that might happen when interacting with an invalid target by inspecting and rejecting incorrect addresses.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaPolicy.sol#L258-L260
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-llama/blob/main/src/LlamaPolicy.sol#L258-L260


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
LlamaPolicy is the central repository that tracks enabled roles for approval and disapproval quantity and sum. When strategies ask for total holders or total quantity, the Llama Policy is returning the stored values in the role Supply state variable.

When each role is setup, it is configured with an expiry timestamp as defined in the below structure.
At the time of setting up the role, the expiration is checked against the block time and the role is configured if it did not expire.
But the role for the policy holder might expire by the next block itself and should disqualify the policy holder from participating in the decision process.

```
struct RoleHolderData {
  uint8 role; // ID of the role to set (uint8 ensures on-chain enumerability when burning policies).
  address policyholder; // Policyholder to assign the role to.
  uint128 quantity; // Quantity of the role to assign to the policyholder, i.e. their (dis)approval quantity.
  uint64 expiration; // When the role expires.
}
```
As and when the role expires, the policy holder should not be accounted under this role. On expiry, the role looses entitlement to contribute to the decisions and hence policy holders.

But, the get Functions like getRoleSupplyAsNumberOfHolders() of LlamaPolicy are not checking for expired roles before returning the values to strategies. Essentially, instead of returning the snapshot, the underlying policy holders and their role's expiry timestamp should be checked to ensure only valid policy holders are participating in the decision process.

This can result in 3 scenarios: 1. Policy holders/Users creating and executing actions can bypass guards if owner initially setGuard for a specific data incorporated in a action. Essentially, users can choose which actionCreation, preAction and postAction guards to execute simply by changing data supplied to correspond to the `bytes4` data selector that has been set by protocol owner to correspond to specific guards instances.
2. Unknowing users that happen to supply same data as other users can have their actions unexpectedly revert or passed due to wrong guards instances applied.
